from pathlib import Path
Path('/tmp/frontend-release-design-astra.md').write_text('''# Selective builds inside the existing release workflow

Keep the current prepare → build → release pipeline and its one complete release transaction. Add one release plan, one backend-build switch, and reuse the existing digest artifact shape. The frontend is always built for every automatic release because its footer embeds the newly allocated version.

## Organizing shape and interfaces

A preparation helper returns a small discriminated plan: `{backend: "build", reason}` or `{backend: "reuse", baseline_source, digests: {server, migrate, cli}}`. The reuse digests are immutable original index digests read directly from a previous published release’s `images.json`. The workflow transports this as compact JSON or an artifact; avoid independent loosely coupled booleans and optional digests. A reusable pure classifier takes event, validated baseline, ancestry, and changed paths; network/git collection stays outside it.

The build action gets `build-backend` default `true`. Guard all three Rust target steps with it, keep frontend unconditional, and validate the input as a strict boolean. Manual AMD64 cache warming and ARM test callers omit the new input and retain their existing all-target behavior. The workflow selects built versus reused backend digests once when constructing the existing full `amd64.json`; the action need not know anything about releases or baseline lookup. Never treat an empty build output as permission to reuse.

## Baseline and conservative selection

On push, retrieve the published latest release and its complete `images.json`, then validate version/tag consistency, a full commit SHA, all four expected same-repository immutable `sha256` references, and published/non-prerelease status. Fetch sufficient Git history and require the recorded source to be an ancestor of the current SHA. Compare that source to the current SHA, never `github.event.before`. Missing release, missing asset, bad JSON/schema, API failure, unresolved source, or nonancestor all select a full build with a concise reason. Existing published release manifests already provide the needed baseline; reserved tags and failed workflow runs are irrelevant.

Permit reuse only when every changed file is in a small explicit safe set: `frontend/**` and `docker/Dockerfile.frontend` initially. Everything else conservatively rebuilds backend. This avoids silently forgetting a backend input when the Dockerfile evolves. Documentation-only commits between releases can cause an unnecessary full build; accept that small tradeoff initially rather than maintaining a second full dependency graph. Use Git diff with rename detection disabled so moves out of backend paths cannot disappear into a frontend-only destination. Empty diffs may reuse a valid baseline (reruns still rebuild the versioned frontend).

A stale latest release from an out-of-order completed run remains safe: it is either an ancestor whose entire subsequent diff is checked, or forces full rebuilding. No concurrency overhaul is needed for this request. Reuse references should remain references to original attested indexes, without resolving their platform child manifests or rewriting provenance. If a referenced registry object is missing at publication, fail safely; optionally preflight availability and choose full rebuilding before invoking the action, but do not silently change the plan after partial publication.

## Release contract and caching

Leave publication’s four-variant loop and server alias update order intact. Every release gets four version tags, four immutable references in `images.json`, and `image.txt`. `images.json.source` means the release source; reused backend OCI revision labels honestly retain their older original build source. Document this explicitly. Preserve all attestations by copying original indexes using the existing imagetools flow.

Separate frontend cache reads/writes into `exposed-frontend-linux-ARCH` and backend into `exposed-backend-linux-ARCH`. All three backend targets share the backend scope and one builder. A transitional old-scope read for backend is optional; frontend must never export into the backend scope. The observed migrate dependency recompilation after frontend export supports this isolation, but selection—not cache success—is what guarantees frontend-only releases skip Rust builds.

## Behavioral checks

Use temporary Git repositories and fixture release metadata to test the planner, with stubbed gh responses for lookup failures. Verify frontend-only changes reuse all three exact backend digests; mixed/Rust/migration/SQLx/shared Docker/action/workflow changes build; a failed backend release followed by a frontend commit builds because the successful baseline predates both; first release builds; malformed/missing/wrong-repository metadata and nonancestor sources build; frontend moves from backend paths build; manual dispatch bypasses reuse regardless of baseline. Test final manifest assembly with known original index digests and assert exactly four entries, unchanged reused strings, and current source/version. Validate workflow/action wiring: all three backend steps conditional, frontend unconditional, default all-build for ARM and manual, publication still emits all four tags. Prefer executable behavior tests over text snapshots alone.

## Alternatives and judgment

Splitting frontend/backend release workflows gives independent build execution but immediately requires a release coordinator, cross-workflow baseline selection, provenance-preserving artifact handoff, and race handling to satisfy the current complete four-image release contract. It is defensible only if releases themselves become independently versioned, which is beyond this request.

A backend/frontend matrix inside the current workflow adds conditional artifacts and merge plumbing with little benefit for frontend-only execution. One guarded action is smaller and preserves backend layer reuse.

The selected design scores strongly on correctness (published ancestor comparison), immutable contract (original refs and all tags), manual/failure safety (default build), maintenance (one switch and one plan), and testability (pure selection plus fixture-backed collection). Its deliberate cost is occasional conservative backend rebuilding after unrelated nonfrontend changes.
''')
